deep.reconstruction:
PART A: orbit of (8) Flora, dated 'Göttingen Jan 7. 1848'. The heading says the orbit was derived from normal places for 1847 Oct 22.5, Nov 20.5 and Dec 19.5, mean Berlin time. Flora was discovered by Hind on 1847 Oct 18. The elements are referred to the epoch 1848 Jan 1.0, mean Berlin time:
- M = 35°53'31.98" (mean anomaly)
- Ω = 110°18'50.8" (ascending node)
- Π = 32°52'1.7" (longitude of perihelion)
- i = 5°52'55.9"
- φ = 9°1'36.87" (eccentricity angle, e = sin φ)
- a = 2.2016851
- μ = 1086.110" per day (mean daily motion)

Derived quantities on the page:
- log e = 9.1956181 (i.e. -10), so e = sin φ = 0.1568983.
- log a = 0.3427552.
- log μ = 3.0358738. My gloss: μ = k/a^(3/2) with Gauss's constant k = 3548.18761" (log k = 3.5500066), giving log μ = 3.5500066 - 1.5·0.3427552.
- Period P = 1296000"/μ = 1193.25 sidereal days.
- Perihelion distance q = a(1-e) = 1.8562443.
- Aphelion distance Q = a(1+e) = 2.5471259.

Gauss then notes that an earlier orbit had been computed from the same data. The only difference was that the precession and nutation corrections to the solar places had been left out 'through carelessness'. Those corrections were -8.24", +4.75" and +0.16" for the three dates. He records the earlier (erroneous) elements for the same epoch:
- M = 35°55'37.28", Ω = 110°19'24.00", Π = 32°47'44.9", i = 5°52'50.7", φ = 9°2'38.89"
- log a = 0.3428256, log μ = 3.0357682.
This log μ again equals 3.5500066 - 1.5·log a.

The resulting changes are ΔM ≈ -2'5", ΔΠ ≈ +4'17" and Δφ ≈ -62". This illustrates how sensitive a short-arc three-place orbit is to arc-second errors in the Sun's places. A small doodle (circle with a loop) at left is not mathematical.

PART B: numerical solution of the quartic t^4·√(1/2) = 2t^3 + t^2 + 12t + 8. This is equivalent to t^4 = √2·(2t^3 + t^2 + 12t + 8).

(i) Trial evaluations. The number √2 appears as 1414 and √(1/2) as 707.
- t = 2: RHS = 16+4+24+8 = 52, and √2·52 = 73.5 (partial products 707 and 28). Compare t^4 = 16.
- t = 3: RHS = 54+9+36+8 = 107, √2·107 = 151.3. Compare t^4 = 81.
- t = 4: RHS = 128+16+48+8 = 200, √2·200 = 282.8. Compare t^4 = 256.
- So the positive root lies a little above 4. The trial values 3.5, 4.1 are also jotted.
- At t = 4.2 a column gives t^4/√2 ≈ 220.0 against RHS = 148.2+17.6+50.4+8 = 224.2. The difference is -4.2, the '4,2' at the top of the column.

(ii) Fixed-point iteration (my description of the scheme): t → F(t) = [√2·(2t^3 + t^2 + 12t + 8)]^(1/4), computed with logarithms.
- t = 4.2: log 224.2 = 2.35064; add log √2 = 0.15051 to get 2.50115; divide by 4 to get 0.62529, so F = 4.2198.
- t = 4.22: 2t^3 = 150.303, t^2 = 17.808, 12t = 50.64, sum 226.751. Then log = 2.35555, +0.15051 = 2.50606, /4 = 0.62652, so F = 4.2317.
- t = 4.26: t^2 = 18.1476, 2t^3 = 154.6176, 12t = 51.12, sum 231.8852. Then log = 2.36527, +0.150515 = 2.515785, /4 = 0.62895, so F = 4.2555.

(iii) Regula falsi on g(t) = F(t) - t, in units of 10^-4.
- g(4.20) = +198, g(4.22) = +117 (scribbles 198, 117), g(4.26) = -45.
- The side computation 117+45 = 162, applied to the interval 40, gives a correction 40·117/162 ≈ 29.
- Result: root t ≈ 4.249 (true root 4.2489).

The crossed-out entries ('225,454', '2 20017', '0.45007') are abandoned trial computations. The purpose of the quartic is not stated. The next page studies families of quartics in u with real and complex roots, so it is likely related algebraic or numerical work rather than part of the Flora orbit.
errors: log 224.2 is written 2.35064. With the exact RHS 224.216 the value is 2.35067. This is a slip of 3 units in the 5th decimal and has no effect on the result 4.2198.

If the transcription '4,2347' (the image for t = 4.22) is what Gauss wrote, it is a slip. His own logarithm 0.62652 gives 4.2317, and only 4.2317 makes his interpolated root 4.249 come out. Most likely it is a misreading of 4.2317.
The orbital arithmetic (e = sin φ, log a, log μ = log k - 1.5 log a, period, q, Q) checks to the last place given. The same relation holds for the earlier orbit's log a and log μ.

I could not decompose the signs and magnitudes of the precession+nutation corrections (-8.24", +4.75", +0.16") from the page alone. Their size is the right order for precession over 0.4–2.3 months plus nutation, but no error is asserted.

results.what: Elliptic orbit elements of minor planet (8) Flora from three normal places (Oct–Dec 1847), with derived period and perihelion/aphelion distances
results.modern_name: Preliminary orbit determination from three observations (Gaussian method), Keplerian elements
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria motus 1809); Flora orbits computed by several astronomers in 1847–48

results.what: Documentation of the effect of omitting precession/nutation reduction of solar coordinates on a three-place orbit (earlier vs corrected elements)
results.modern_name: Sensitivity of initial orbit determination to reference-frame reduction errors

results.what: Numerical root of t^4/√2 = 2t^3+t^2+12t+8 by logarithmic fixed-point iteration t ← (√2·RHS)^(1/4) followed by regula falsi, giving t ≈ 4.249
results.modern_name: Fixed-point iteration with secant/regula falsi interpolation
results.usually_credited_to: classical (regula falsi ancient; iteration standard by 18th c.)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine orbit computations for a newly discovered asteroid, an activity well known for Gauss in 1847–48. The quartic is solved by standard iteration and regula falsi. The only mildly interesting detail is Gauss's candid record of an orbit spoiled by forgetting precession and nutation in the solar places.

checkable.asserts: log mu = log k - 1.5 log a (Gauss constant in arcsec)

transcription_corrections: '4,2347' (iterate for t = 4.220) should almost certainly read 4,2317; this follows from 10^0.62652 and the final interpolation to 4.249.
'79,5' should be 73,5 (√2·52 = 73.54, from partial products 707 and 28).
'Ein frühere Bahn' reads 'Eine frühere Bahn'; 'Sonnenoertern' is correct.
The marginal '198, 117, 45, 162' are the regula-falsi residuals F(t)-t in units of 1e-4 (and their sum 117+45), not independent data.
